The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ has a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures: if finite measures $\mu,\nu$ agree on $\mathcal A$, then $\mu=\nu$. In particular it determines probability measures.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

For any product-measurable $A$, the section integrals are measurable by [F4]. If $Q(A)=0$, then $R(x,A_x)=0$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ by [F5]; intersecting with the conull kernel-domination set gives $M(x,A_x)=0$ there, hence $P(A)=0$. Thus $P\ll Q$.

By [F6], choose a product-measurable density $h=dP/dQ$. On $N=\{h<0\}$, positivity of $P$ gives $0\le P(N)=\int_Nh\,dQ=-\int_Nh^-\,dQ$, so [F5] makes $h^-=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere on $N$. The Borel positive-part map preserves measurability by [F9], so replacing $h$ by $h^+=\max(h,0)$ leaves the density unchanged $Q$-almost everywhere and makes it nonnegative.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a countable measure-determining algebra on $F$ from [F7], containing $F$. For each $B\in\mathcal C$ and $D\in\mathcal E$, the rectangle laws and density identity [F8] give $\int_D M(x,B)\lambda(dx)=P(D\times B)=\int_D(\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy))\lambda(dx)$. Both integrands are measurable by [F2] and [F4] and integrable because their integrals over $E$ are at most one. Uniqueness of Radon–Nikodym densities in [F6] makes them equal $\lambda$-almost everywhere for each fixed $B$.

Intersect the conull sets from step 3.1 over the countable algebra $\mathcal C$. For each $x$ in the intersection, the section $h(x,\cdot)$ is measurable by [F10], so [F11] makes $B\mapsto\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy)$ a measure. The kernel section $M(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure by [F2]. These two measures agree on $\mathcal C$ and have total mass one because $F\in\mathcal C$ and step 3.1 includes $B=F$. The measure-determining property [F7] makes them equal on every $B\in\mathcal F$, with the same exceptional null set for all $B$. Taking $r=h$ proves the assertion.

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

In the residual branch, write $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$ and $r_j=Np_j-q_j$. The remainder $R=\sum_jr_j=N-\sum_jq_j$ is an integer. If $R=0$, every $r_j=0$ and $C_j=q_j=Np_j$; if $R>0$, then $C_j=q_j+\sum_{\ell=1}^{R}\mathbf 1_{\{K_\ell=j\}}$ with each indicator having conditional expectation $r_j/R$, so $\mathbb E[C_j\mid a]=q_j+R(r_j/R)=Np_j$.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish the same conditional expected-count identity for both schemes in the procedure, completing the assertion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Fix $N\ge1$ and nonnegative input weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$. Let $p$ be the normalized probability vector, with the uniform fallback when all weights vanish, and let $C_j$ be the offspring count from [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional on the input weights, for either scheme and every $1\le j\le N$,
$$\mathbb E[C_j\mid a_1,\ldots,a_N]=Np_j.$$
This assertion concerns the counts only; it gives no variance comparison for arbitrary weights.

Assume AC and the finite-horizon setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For $1\le k\le T$ and every nonnegative product-measurable $\varphi:\mathsf X_{0:k}\to[0,\infty]$,
$$\gamma_k(\varphi)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:k-1}}\gamma_{k-1}(dx_{0:k-1})\int_{\mathsf X_k}G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})M_k(x_{k-1},dx_k),$$
with equality in $[0,\infty]$.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]] through a fixed horizon $t\le T$. Let $\nu_0$ be a proposal probability on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le t$ let $R_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be proposal probability kernels. Define $Q_s(dx_{0:s})=\nu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^sR_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$. Suppose $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$, and for each $k$ suppose $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of $Q_{k-1}$. Choose a measurable version $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and, using [[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels]], measurable versions $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ for these preceding-state marginals.

Then $\gamma_s\ll Q_s$ for every $s\le t$, with product density
$$W_s(x_{0:s})=G_0(x_0)\rho_0(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^sG_k(x_k)r_k(x_{k-1},x_k).$$
That is, $\gamma_s(A)=\int_AW_s\,dQ_s$ for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathsf X_{0:s}$. If $0<Z_s<\infty$, the normalized path target has density $W_s/Z_s$ with respect to $Q_s$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$
Assume AC. For every real integrable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and every sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, a conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ exists.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $P(A)=\int_Au\,dQ$ for every measurable $A$, with $u\ge0$, choose simple $g_n\uparrow g$ by [F15]. The simple-function identity [F14] gives $\int g_n\,dP=\int g_nu\,dQ$ for each $n$, and [F16] on both sides yields $\int g\,dP=\int gu\,dQ$, allowing infinity. This applies to the initial law pair and, for almost every preceding proposal state, to each transition-kernel pair in [F5]. At time zero, the algorithm gives $\widehat\gamma_0^N(\varphi)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^NG_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)\varphi(X_0^i)$, with zero-weight terms interpreted by the nonnegative-integral convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. Each $X_0^i$ has law $\nu_0$, so [F6], finite-sum linearity [F7], and the just-proved extension give $\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_0^N(\varphi)]=\int G_0\rho_0\varphi\,d\nu_0=\gamma_0(\varphi)$. The finite target integral makes this random variable integrable.

Every time-zero particle path has law $Q_0$. Inductively, resampling copies only paths already present. If $Q_k(A)=0$, its iterated-kernel formula from [F12] and [F13] gives $R_k(x,A_x)=0$ for $Q_{k-1}$-almost every history; propagation therefore avoids $A$ almost surely whenever every previous particle path avoids each fixed $Q_{k-1}$-null set. Thus sampled parent states lie in the proposal-marginal full sets where the kernel derivatives apply. Each initial or kernel derivative has reference integral one by [F5]. If such a nonnegative derivative were infinite on a set of positive reference measure, its integral would exceed every finite bound; hence all these derivatives are finite almost everywhere. The potentials are finite-valued, so all particle weights are finite almost surely.

Write $\mathcal F_{k-1}$ for the previous particle histories and weights. Let $H_k$ be the integral of $\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)$ against the algorithm's conditional finite-step transition law. By [F3], the expected number of children from parent $j$ is $N\bar w_{k-1}^j$. For each parent outside the exceptional proposal-marginal null set, apply the simple-approximation extension in step 1.1 to the nonnegative measurable function $x_k\mapsto G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})$; the setwise identity in [F5] then gives $\int G_k\varphi\,r_k\,dR_k=\int G_k\varphi\,dM_k$, including infinite values. Integrating each child's incremental weight and summing the expected counts therefore gives $H_k=\widehat\gamma_{k-1}^N(g_k)$, where $g_k(x_{0:k-1})=\int G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})M_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$. If the previous normalizer estimate is zero, both sides vanish by the algorithm's zero-weight convention. Measurability follows from [F11]. This is initially a nonnegative conditional-kernel integral, not yet an $L^1$ conditional expectation.

By [F4], the target integral of $g_k$ is $\gamma_{k-1}(g_k)=\gamma_k(\varphi)<\infty$. The induction hypothesis therefore gives $\mathbb E[H_k]=\gamma_k(\varphi)$. For every prior event $B\in\mathcal F_{k-1}$, the ordered joint law of the prior histories and the algorithm's conditional finite-step transition law [F12], integrated with the nonnegative integrand $\mathbf1_B\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)$, gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)]=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_BH_k].$ This identity is valid before any integrability assumption, by nonnegative iterated integration. Taking $B=\Omega$ shows that $\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)$ has finite expectation $\gamma_k(\varphi)$, so it is in $L^1$; $H_k$ is also in $L^1$ by its finite expectation. Thus the event identities and measurability make $H_k$ a version of $\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]$ by [F2] and [F10]. The tower property [F9] now yields $\mathbb E[\widehat\gamma_k^N(\varphi)]=\gamma_k(\varphi)$, completing the induction step.

Apply the established identity at $k=t$ to the constant function $\varphi=1$. Then $\widehat\gamma_t^N(1)=\widehat Z_t\widehat\pi_t^N(1)=\widehat Z_t$, while $\gamma_t(1)=Z_t$, proving the stated normalizer unbiasedness.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{f\tilde p\ne0\}$ and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are IID with law $Q$. For the ordinary importance sampling estimator in [[alg-importance-sampling]],
$$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\mathsf X_0=\{*\}$ and $\mathsf X_1=\{a,b\}$. Take $\mu_0=\nu_0=\delta_*$, $M_1(*,\{a\})=M_1(*,\{b\})=1/2$, $R_1(*,\{a\})=1$, $R_1(*,\{b\})=0$, and $G_0=G_1=1$. By [F1], $\gamma_1$ is the transition law itself, $Z_1=1$, and the normalized target assigns mass $1/2$ to $b$.

The support premise fails because $M_1(*,\{b\})=1/2$ while $R_1(*,\{b\})=0$. A proposal path drawn from $Q_1=\nu_0R_1$ equals $(*,a)$ with probability one, so every empirical measure formed from such paths assigns mass zero to the event $\{x_1=b\}$.

If a kernel derivative $r_1$ represented $M_1(*,\cdot)$ with respect to $R_1(*,\cdot)$, then $M_1(*,\{b\})=\int_{\{b\}}r_1(*,y)R_1(*,dy)=0$, contradicting the value $1/2$. Thus the required importance weight does not exist on this target-positive, proposal-null set, and the false claim fails.
